cards.question_text: What is the primary purpose of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)?
choices: To provide a voluntary framework of standards, guidelines, and best practices for managing cybersecurity risk
To mandate specific encryption algorithms that all US organizations must use
To certify products as secure through laboratory testing and validation
To provide a legally binding set of regulations for data breach notification
cards.answer: To provide a voluntary framework of standards, guidelines, and best practices for managing cybersecurity risk
cards.explanation_correct: The NIST CSF is a voluntary framework that provides organizations with standards, guidelines, and best practices to manage and reduce cybersecurity risk. It organizes security activities into five core functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. It is not a legal mandate or a product certification — it is a risk management guidance document.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: The NIST CSF does not mandate specific algorithms, certify products (that is FIPS/Common Criteria), or create legal regulations. Its defining characteristic is that it is voluntary guidance for improving cybersecurity risk management across any organization, regardless of size or sector.

cards.question_text: What is the difference between ISO 27001 and ISO 27002?
choices: ISO 27001 defines the requirements for an Information Security Management System (ISMS); ISO 27002 provides a code of practice with detailed security controls
ISO 27001 covers physical security; ISO 27002 covers network security
ISO 27001 is for governments; ISO 27002 is for private companies
ISO 27001 is the European version; ISO 27002 is the American version
cards.answer: ISO 27001 defines the requirements for an Information Security Management System (ISMS); ISO 27002 provides a code of practice with detailed security controls
cards.explanation_correct: ISO/IEC 27001 is the international standard that specifies the requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving an Information Security Management System (ISMS). It is certifiable — organizations can be audited against it. ISO/IEC 27002 is a companion standard that provides a code of practice listing detailed security controls (Annex A controls) and guidance on how to implement them.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: The distinction is not about physical vs network, government vs private, or regional versions. ISO 27001 is the management system standard (requirements, certifiable), while ISO 27002 is the operational guidance (how to implement controls). Together they form a complementary pair — 27001 tells you what to do, 27002 tells you how.

cards.question_text: A company wants to benchmark its security posture against a prioritized set of actionable controls and measure improvement over time. Which framework is best suited for this purpose, and why?
choices: CIS Controls, because they provide a prioritized, actionable list of security best practices organized into Implementation Groups (IG1, IG2, IG3) based on organizational risk profile
PCI DSS, because it provides universal security requirements applicable to all industries
ITIL, because it focuses on IT service management rather than security
COBIT, because it is primarily a financial auditing framework
cards.answer: CIS Controls, because they provide a prioritized, actionable list of security best practices organized into Implementation Groups (IG1, IG2, IG3) based on organizational risk profile
cards.explanation_correct: The CIS (Center for Internet Security) Controls are a prioritized set of actionable security best practices that organizations can implement to defend against common threats. They are organized into three Implementation Groups (IG1 for basic cyber hygiene, IG2 for mature organizations, IG3 for sophisticated defenders), allowing organizations to benchmark and incrementally improve. The prioritized, actionable nature makes them ideal for measuring security posture improvement.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: PCI DSS is specific to payment card data, not universal. ITIL is IT service management, not cybersecurity. COBIT is IT governance, not specifically security benchmarking. Only the CIS Controls combine prioritization, actionability, and tiered implementation groups specifically designed for security posture measurement.

cards.question_text: A security team is mapping adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) to understand how attackers operate and to improve detection capabilities. Which framework should they use?
choices: MITRE ATT&CK, a globally accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations
NIST CSF, because it categorizes security activities into five core functions
ISO 27001, because it defines ISMS requirements for certification
OWASP Top 10, because it lists the most critical web application security risks
cards.answer: MITRE ATT&CK, a globally accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations
cards.explanation_correct: MITRE ATT&CK is a curated knowledge base that documents adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) observed in real-world attacks. It organizes techniques into a matrix of tactics (the 'why' — objectives like initial access, persistence, exfiltration) and techniques (the 'how' — specific methods). Security teams use it to map detections, test defenses, and understand adversary behavior patterns.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: NIST CSF organizes security functions (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) but does not catalog adversary TTPs. ISO 27001 is an ISMS standard, not a threat intelligence framework. OWASP Top 10 covers web app vulnerabilities, not broad adversary tactics. Only MITRE ATT&CK specifically catalogs real-world adversary behaviors.

cards.question_text: A mid-sized financial services company must comply with multiple requirements: they process credit cards, operate under a regulatory framework requiring formal ISMS certification, and want to benchmark their security controls against industry best practices. Which combination of frameworks should they adopt, and what is each one's role?
choices: PCI DSS for payment card compliance, ISO 27001 for ISMS certification, and CIS Controls for benchmarking security posture — each addresses a different need
NIST CSF alone, because it covers all compliance, certification, and benchmarking requirements in a single framework
COBIT for everything, because it is the most comprehensive IT governance framework
MITRE ATT&CK for compliance and ISO 27001 for benchmarking, since both are certifiable standards
cards.answer: PCI DSS for payment card compliance, ISO 27001 for ISMS certification, and CIS Controls for benchmarking security posture — each addresses a different need
cards.explanation_correct: No single framework covers all needs. PCI DSS is mandatory for organizations processing credit cards and specifies payment data security requirements. ISO 27001 provides a certifiable ISMS framework that satisfies regulatory requirements for formal security management. CIS Controls provide prioritized, actionable security best practices for benchmarking and improving posture. Using all three ensures compliance, certification, and practical improvement are each addressed.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: No single framework is comprehensive enough — NIST CSF is voluntary guidance, not certifiable or PCI-compliant. COBIT is IT governance, not security-specific. MITRE ATT&CK is threat intelligence, not a compliance or certification framework. The correct approach combines purpose-built frameworks: regulatory compliance (PCI DSS), management certification (ISO 27001), and operational benchmarking (CIS Controls).

cards.question_text: What is the difference between a threat and a vulnerability?
choices: A threat is a potential danger that can exploit a vulnerability; a vulnerability is a weakness that could allow a threat to cause harm
A threat is a weakness in a system; a vulnerability is an active attack in progress
A threat is always external; a vulnerability is always internal
A threat is a security control; a vulnerability is the absence of encryption
cards.answer: A threat is a potential danger that can exploit a vulnerability; a vulnerability is a weakness that could allow a threat to cause harm
cards.explanation_correct: A threat is any potential danger or event that could exploit a vulnerability to compromise security (e.g., a hacker, malware, natural disaster). A vulnerability is a weakness, flaw, or gap in a system's security that a threat could exploit (e.g., unpatched software, misconfiguration, weak password). Risk exists when a threat has the capability and opportunity to exploit a vulnerability — risk = threat × vulnerability × impact.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Threats and vulnerabilities are not the same thing, nor are they defined by internal/external origin. A threat is not a control, and a vulnerability is not specifically about encryption. The key relationship is: threats exploit vulnerabilities to create risk. Without a vulnerability, a threat cannot cause harm, and without a threat, a vulnerability is merely a latent weakness.

cards.question_text: What is residual risk?
choices: The risk that remains after security controls have been implemented and risk treatment measures applied
The risk that was present before any security controls were implemented
The risk that only affects residual systems like legacy hardware
The risk associated with deleting old data and residual files
cards.answer: The risk that remains after security controls have been implemented and risk treatment measures applied
cards.explanation_correct: Residual risk is the portion of risk that remains after all risk treatment measures (controls, mitigations, transfers, etc.) have been applied. No security control eliminates 100% of risk — there is always some remaining risk. Management must formally accept residual risk as part of the risk management process. The formula is: residual risk = inherent risk - risk reduction from controls.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Residual risk is not the risk before controls (that is inherent risk), not specific to legacy systems, and not about data deletion. The term 'residual' refers to what remains after treatment. Understanding residual risk is critical because management must decide whether the remaining risk is acceptable or if additional controls are needed.

cards.question_text: A company identifies a vulnerability in its web application that could lead to data exposure. The risk score is calculated as High. However, fixing the vulnerability requires taking the application offline for 8 hours during peak business season, causing significant revenue loss. The CISO decides to accept the risk for now and schedule the fix during the next maintenance window. What risk treatment strategy is this?
choices: Risk acceptance — the organization acknowledges the risk and chooses to tolerate it temporarily without additional controls
Risk mitigation — the organization reduces the risk by scheduling a fix
Risk transference — the organization transfers the risk to the maintenance team
Risk avoidance — the organization avoids the risk by not fixing it
cards.answer: Risk acceptance — the organization acknowledges the risk and chooses to tolerate it temporarily without additional controls
cards.explanation_correct: Risk acceptance is a risk treatment strategy where the organization formally acknowledges that a risk exists and decides to tolerate it, typically because the cost of mitigation exceeds the potential impact, or because business priorities make immediate remediation impractical. In this case, the CISO accepts the risk temporarily due to the business cost of downtime. Risk acceptance should always be a documented, formal management decision, not an informal choice.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: This is not mitigation (no control is reducing the risk now), not transference (no insurance or third party is absorbing the risk), and not avoidance (avoidance would mean eliminating the activity that creates the risk, e.g., shutting down the application). Scheduling a future fix does not constitute mitigation in the present — the current decision is to accept the risk until the maintenance window.

cards.question_text: An organization purchases a cybersecurity insurance policy that covers data breach response costs, legal fees, and regulatory fines up to $5 million. Which risk treatment strategy is being applied, and what is its key limitation?
choices: Risk transference — the financial impact is transferred to the insurer, but the reputational and operational damage remains with the organization
Risk mitigation — the insurance policy reduces the likelihood of a breach occurring
Risk avoidance — by having insurance, the organization avoids all breach consequences
Risk acceptance — the organization accepts that breaches will happen and does nothing else
cards.answer: Risk transference — the financial impact is transferred to the insurer, but the reputational and operational damage remains with the organization
cards.explanation_correct: Risk transference (or sharing) shifts the financial burden of a risk to a third party, typically through insurance or contracts. Cybersecurity insurance transfers the financial costs of a breach (response, legal, fines) to the insurer. However, the key limitation is that insurance only covers financial impact — reputational damage, loss of customer trust, operational disruption, and regulatory scrutiny remain with the organization. Transference does not reduce likelihood or eliminate all consequences.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Insurance does not mitigate (it does not reduce likelihood or impact of the breach itself — it only covers costs after the fact). It is not avoidance (the organization still faces the risk) and not acceptance (active steps are taken to transfer financial risk). The critical distinction is that transference moves financial consequences but cannot transfer reputational or operational impacts.

cards.question_text: A hospital's risk assessment identifies that an outdated MRI scheduling system has a critical unpatched vulnerability. The system cannot be patched because the vendor no longer supports it, replacing it costs $800K and takes 6 months, and the vulnerability could allow an attacker to alter patient appointment data (integrity risk). The hospital operates 24/7 and cannot take the MRI scheduling system offline. Which combination of risk treatments provides the best immediate risk reduction while planning for long-term remediation?
choices: Implement compensating controls (network segmentation to isolate the system, strict firewall rules, enhanced logging and monitoring) now, transfer residual risk via cyber insurance, and plan system replacement as a long-term mitigation project
Accept the risk entirely since the system cannot be patched and the hospital cannot go offline
Avoid the risk by immediately decommissioning the MRI scheduling system and reverting to paper-based scheduling
Transfer the risk entirely to the vendor by threatening legal action for end-of-life support
cards.answer: Implement compensating controls (network segmentation to isolate the system, strict firewall rules, enhanced logging and monitoring) now, transfer residual risk via cyber insurance, and plan system replacement as a long-term mitigation project
cards.explanation_correct: When a vulnerability cannot be directly remediated (no patch available) and the system cannot be taken offline, compensating controls provide the best immediate risk reduction. Network segmentation isolates the vulnerable system from the broader network, firewall rules restrict access to only necessary traffic, and enhanced logging/monitoring enables rapid detection of exploitation attempts. Cyber insurance transfers the residual financial risk. The long-term mitigation (system replacement) addresses the root cause. This multi-layered approach combines compensating controls (reduce), transference (share), and mitigation (eliminate) appropriately.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Full risk acceptance is irresponsible when compensating controls can reduce the risk. Decommissioning the system (avoidance) would severely disrupt patient care — a worse outcome than the security risk. Legal threats against the vendor do not transfer the operational risk and do not protect the system. Only the combination of compensating controls + transference + planned remediation provides layered, practical risk reduction for an irreplaceable legacy system.

cards.question_text: What distinguishes an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) from other types of threat actors?
choices: APTs are well-resourced, highly skilled actors (often nation-state sponsored) who maintain long-term, stealthy access to a target network to exfiltrate data over time
APTs are amateur hackers who use automated tools to scan for vulnerable systems
APTs are insider threats who already have legitimate access to the network
APTs are opportunistic criminals who deploy ransomware for quick financial gain
cards.answer: APTs are well-resourced, highly skilled actors (often nation-state sponsored) who maintain long-term, stealthy access to a target network to exfiltrate data over time
cards.explanation_correct: An Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) is characterized by three key attributes: Advanced (using sophisticated techniques and zero-day exploits), Persistent (maintaining long-term, stealthy access to the target), and Threat (a well-resourced, organized adversary, often nation-state or state-sponsored). APTs prioritize stealth and data exfiltration over immediate disruption — their goal is typically espionage, intellectual property theft, or long-term surveillance rather than quick financial gain.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: APTs are not amateurs (that describes script kiddies), not insiders (though APTs may recruit insiders), and not opportunistic criminals seeking quick payouts (that describes typical ransomware operators). The defining characteristics are sophistication, stealth, persistence, and a long-term strategic objective — not speed or opportunism.

cards.question_text: What is the difference between a hacktivist and a cybercriminal in terms of motivation?
choices: Hacktivists are motivated by political, social, or ideological causes; cybercriminals are motivated by financial gain
Hacktivists are motivated by financial gain; cybercriminals are motivated by political causes
Hacktivists and cybercriminals have identical motivations — both seek profit
Hacktivists are always nation-state actors; cybercriminals are always lone individuals
cards.answer: Hacktivists are motivated by political, social, or ideological causes; cybercriminals are motivated by financial gain
cards.explanation_correct: Hacktivists (hacker + activist) use cyber attacks to advance political, social, or ideological causes. Their attacks often involve website defacement, DDoS attacks, or data leaks meant to embarrass or disrupt their targets (e.g., Anonymous, Lizard Squad). Cybercriminals are motivated primarily by financial gain — they steal data for sale, deploy ransomware, or commit fraud for monetary profit. Understanding motivation helps predict attack methods and targets.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: The motivations are not reversed, nor are they identical. While there can be overlap (a hacktivist may also profit), the primary distinguishing factor is motivation: ideology (hacktivist) vs profit (cybercriminal). Neither is exclusively nation-state or lone individual — both can operate in groups. Motivation is the key differentiator, not skill level or organization size.

cards.question_text: A disgruntled former system administrator, whose access was supposed to be revoked on their last day, uses a backdoor account they created before leaving to log into the company's customer database and download sensitive records. What type of threat actor is this, and what was the failure in the offboarding process?
choices: Insider threat (malicious insider); the failure was incomplete access revocation — dormant/backdoor accounts were not identified and disabled during offboarding
External threat actor; the failure was a weak firewall that allowed the attacker through
APT; the failure was lack of zero-day exploit detection
Hacktivist; the failure was not monitoring the company's social media for ideological threats
cards.answer: Insider threat (malicious insider); the failure was incomplete access revocation — dormant/backdoor accounts were not identified and disabled during offboarding
cards.explanation_correct: This is a malicious insider threat — the attacker was a former employee with legitimate knowledge of the systems who used unauthorized access they pre-positioned. The offboarding failure was incomplete access revocation: the official account was disabled, but the backdoor account (created covertly) was not discovered. Proper offboarding should include auditing for unauthorized accounts, reviewing recently created accounts, and revoking all access including SSH keys, VPN credentials, and API tokens — not just the primary user account.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: This is not an external attacker (the threat actor had insider knowledge and pre-positioned access), not an APT (the attacker is a known former employee, not a sophisticated nation-state group), and not a hacktivist (the motivation appears to be personal grievance, not ideology). The root cause is an offboarding process gap — backdoor account detection — not a network perimeter failure.

cards.question_text: A security analyst notices a series of phishing emails targeting the company's finance department. The emails appear to come from the CEO and urgently request wire transfers to a 'new vendor.' The sender addresses are lookalike domains (e.g., ceo@company-lnvoice.com instead of ceo@company-invoice.com). What attack vector and social engineering technique is being used?
choices: Spear phishing using CEO fraud (whaling) with domain typosquatting — targeting specific individuals in finance with authority to authorize transfers
Mass phishing using generic emails sent to all employees regardless of role
Smishing (SMS phishing) targeting employees' personal phones
Watering hole attack targeting a website the finance team frequently visits
cards.answer: Spear phishing using CEO fraud (whaling) with domain typosquatting — targeting specific individuals in finance with authority to authorize transfers
cards.explanation_correct: This is a spear phishing attack using whaling (CEO fraud) — a targeted social engineering attack where the attacker impersonates a high-ranking executive (the CEO) to pressure employees with financial authority into making wire transfers. The lookalike domain (typosquatting/homoglyph attack) makes the email appear legitimate at a glance. Spear phishing is targeted (specific finance employees, not mass), and whaling specifically targets high-value victims or impersonates executives. Business Email Compromise (BEC) is the broader category for this attack type.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: This is not mass phishing (the emails are targeted at the finance department specifically), not smishing (email, not SMS), and not a watering hole attack (no compromised website is involved). The combination of executive impersonation + lookalike domains + targeting employees with transfer authority is the hallmark of whaling/CEO fraud via spear phishing.

cards.question_text: A defense contractor discovers that an APT group has been embedded in their network for 14 months. The attackers entered through a spear phishing email to an engineer, established persistence via scheduled tasks, moved laterally using stolen credentials obtained via Mimikatz, and exfiltrated classified design documents through DNS tunneling to evade DLP controls. Which sequence of attack phases best describes this intrusion, and what defensive control would have been most effective at the earliest stage?
choices: Phishing (initial access) → Persistence (scheduled tasks) → Credential theft (Mimikatz) → Lateral movement → Data exfiltration (DNS tunneling); security awareness training + email filtering would have been most effective at the initial access stage
Network scan → Brute force → Malware deployment → Data destruction; a firewall would have been most effective
Physical breach → Hardware tampering → Data theft; biometric access controls would have been most effective
Insider collusion → Data copy → Physical removal; badge logging would have been most effective
cards.answer: Phishing (initial access) → Persistence (scheduled tasks) → Credential theft (Mimikatz) → Lateral movement → Data exfiltration (DNS tunneling); security awareness training + email filtering would have been most effective at the initial access stage
cards.explanation_correct: This intrusion follows the classic APT kill chain: spear phishing for initial access, scheduled tasks for persistence, Mimikatz for credential theft, lateral movement using those credentials, and DNS tunneling for covert exfiltration. The earliest and most effective intervention point is the initial access stage — robust email filtering (to block the phishing email) and security awareness training (so the engineer recognizes and reports the phishing attempt) would have prevented the entire chain. Each subsequent phase becomes harder to detect and stop, making prevention at initial access the highest-impact control.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: This was not a network scan/brute force (the entry was via phishing), not a physical breach (it was a remote intrusion), and not insider collusion (the engineer was an unwitting victim). The kill chain begins with social engineering, not technical exploitation. While controls at every stage matter (EDR for persistence detection, credential guarding for Mimikatz, network monitoring for lateral movement, DNS analysis for tunneling), prevention at initial access has the highest return on investment because it stops the chain before it starts.

cards.question_text: What is the Zero Trust security model, and how does it differ from a traditional perimeter-based security model?
choices: Zero Trust assumes no user or device is trusted by default, requiring continuous authentication and authorization for every access request regardless of network location; traditional perimeter security trusts everything inside the network boundary
Zero Trust requires zero security controls, trusting users to self-regulate; perimeter security uses firewalls only
Zero Trust encrypts all data at rest; perimeter security encrypts data in transit
Zero Trust only applies to cloud environments; perimeter security only applies to on-premises networks
cards.answer: Zero Trust assumes no user or device is trusted by default, requiring continuous authentication and authorization for every access request regardless of network location; traditional perimeter security trusts everything inside the network boundary
cards.explanation_correct: Zero Trust is a security model based on the principle 'never trust, always verify.' It eliminates implicit trust based on network location — even users and devices inside the corporate network must authenticate and be authorized for every access request. Core principles include identity-based access, least privilege, micro-segmentation, and continuous monitoring. Traditional perimeter security (castle-and-moat) assumes that anything inside the network boundary is trustworthy, which fails once an attacker breaches the perimeter.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Zero Trust does not mean 'zero controls' (it requires more controls, just applied differently). It is not about encryption location, and it is not limited to cloud or on-premises — it is an architectural philosophy applicable to any environment. The fundamental shift is from location-based trust (inside = trusted) to identity-based trust (verify every request, regardless of location).

cards.question_text: What is defense in depth, and why is it important in cybersecurity?
choices: Defense in depth is a strategy that uses multiple layers of security controls so that if one layer fails, others remain to protect the system; it is important because no single control is 100% effective
Defense in depth means using only encryption to protect data at all depths of the network
Defense in depth is a military strategy unrelated to cybersecurity
Defense in depth means deploying a single very strong firewall deep in the network core
cards.answer: Defense in depth is a strategy that uses multiple layers of security controls so that if one layer fails, others remain to protect the system; it is important because no single control is 100% effective
cards.explanation_correct: Defense in depth is a layered security approach where multiple independent controls protect assets at different levels — physical security, network perimeter (firewall), network segmentation, host security (hardening, EDR), application security, and data security (encryption). If one control fails or is bypassed, other layers continue to provide protection. It is important because every security control has weaknesses, and attackers often find ways around individual controls — layering reduces the probability of a complete breach.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Defense in depth is not about encryption alone, not exclusive to the military (though the concept originated there, it is a core cybersecurity principle), and not about a single strong control. The essence is redundancy and layering — diverse control types across multiple layers so that the failure of any single control does not result in total compromise.

cards.question_text: A company hosts its public-facing web server in a DMZ (demilitarized zone) and its internal database server on the internal network. The web server needs to query the database. A security architect recommends that only the web server's IP can connect to the database on port 3306, and the database server has no direct internet access. Which security architecture principles are being applied?
choices: Network segmentation with a DMZ, principle of least privilege (only the web server can access the database on a specific port), and attack surface reduction (no direct internet access for the database)
Zero Trust architecture with continuous authentication for every database query
Defense in depth using only encryption to protect database traffic
Risk transference by placing the database in the DMZ alongside the web server
cards.answer: Network segmentation with a DMZ, principle of least privilege (only the web server can access the database on a specific port), and attack surface reduction (no direct internet access for the database)
cards.explanation_correct: Three principles are at work: (1) Network segmentation — the DMZ isolates public-facing servers from the internal network, limiting what an attacker can reach if the web server is compromised. (2) Least privilege — the firewall rule restricts database access to only the web server's IP on a specific port, not any internal host. (3) Attack surface reduction — the database has no internet route, meaning external attackers cannot reach it directly. Together these controls ensure that even if the web server is breached, the database is not directly exposed to the internet and is only reachable from one known host.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: This is not Zero Trust (which would require continuous identity verification for every query, not just network-level IP filtering). It is not defense in depth via encryption alone (segmentation, not encryption, is the primary control described). The database is NOT in the DMZ (it is on the internal network), so this is not risk transference. The scenario specifically demonstrates segmentation + least privilege + attack surface reduction.

cards.question_text: An organization is implementing Zero Trust architecture. They want to ensure that a user accessing a sensitive financial application from their laptop is continuously evaluated for access. Which combination of controls best implements the Zero Trust principle of continuous verification?
choices: Multi-factor authentication at login, device posture checking (is the laptop managed, patched, and running EDR?), contextual access policies (user role, location, time), and continuous session monitoring with re-authentication for sensitive actions
A strong firewall at the network perimeter and VPN access for all remote users
Single sign-on with a long session timeout (8 hours) so users do not need to re-authenticate frequently
Network segmentation alone, placing the financial application on an isolated VLAN
cards.answer: Multi-factor authentication at login, device posture checking (is the laptop managed, patched, and running EDR?), contextual access policies (user role, location, time), and continuous session monitoring with re-authentication for sensitive actions
cards.explanation_correct: Zero Trust requires continuous verification using multiple signals: who the user is (MFA), the health/trust of their device (posture checking), contextual factors (role, location, time of access), and ongoing session monitoring with step-up authentication for sensitive operations. This multi-signal approach means access is never granted permanently — it is continuously re-evaluated. If any signal degrades (e.g., device becomes non-compliant, user changes location), access can be revoked or restricted in real time.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: A firewall + VPN is traditional perimeter security, not Zero Trust (it grants broad network access after a single authentication). A long SSO session timeout is the opposite of continuous verification (it reduces re-authentication). VLAN segmentation alone is a network control, not identity-centric verification. Zero Trust is about continuous, multi-factor evaluation of every access request — not a single network boundary or session.

cards.question_text: A cloud-native company hosts microservices across multiple cloud providers. An attacker compromises a single microservice via a vulnerable API endpoint. Under a traditional flat network architecture, this compromise could allow lateral movement to all other microservices. Under a Zero Trust architecture with micro-segmentation, what prevents this lateral movement, and what trade-offs does the organization face?
choices: Each microservice is in its own micro-segment with its own identity and access policies — services must mutually authenticate (e.g., via mTLS) and be explicitly authorized to communicate; trade-offs include increased operational complexity, performance overhead from per-connection authentication, and difficulty in troubleshooting service-to-service connectivity
A single centralized firewall blocks all lateral movement automatically with no trade-offs
Encryption of all traffic prevents the attacker from understanding other services, with no performance trade-offs
Moving all services to a single cloud provider eliminates lateral movement risk entirely
cards.answer: Each microservice is in its own micro-segment with its own identity and access policies — services must mutually authenticate (e.g., via mTLS) and be explicitly authorized to communicate; trade-offs include increased operational complexity, performance overhead from per-connection authentication, and difficulty in troubleshooting service-to-service connectivity
cards.explanation_correct: In a Zero Trust micro-segmented architecture, each microservice operates in its own isolated segment with a unique identity. Services must mutually authenticate (typically via mutual TLS / mTLS) and be explicitly authorized before communicating — there is no implicit trust based on network co-location. If one service is compromised, the attacker cannot reach other services without separately authenticating to each one. The trade-offs are real: per-connection authentication adds latency, managing hundreds of service identities and policies increases operational complexity, and debugging service mesh connectivity issues is significantly harder than in a flat network. The security benefit (blast radius containment) must be weighed against these costs.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: No single firewall automatically prevents all lateral movement without trade-offs — micro-segmentation requires identity-level controls, not just network rules. Encryption alone prevents eavesdropping but does not prevent an authenticated attacker from moving between services. Consolidating to one cloud provider does not eliminate lateral movement — the risk exists within any shared environment. Only micro-segmentation with mutual authentication contains the blast radius, and the trade-offs (complexity, performance, troubleshooting) are an inherent part of the architecture.
